title: Financial Assistance Scheme Eligibility
statement:
A government agency runs several financial assistance schemes. You are building the part of the system that tells each applicant which schemes they qualify for.

Write def solution(applicants, schemes).

  • Each applicant is {"id": str, "employment_status": "employed" or "unemployed", "household": [{"relation": str, "age": int}, ...], "monthly_income": int}. household lists the people living with the applicant, not the applicant.
  • Each scheme is {"id": str, "criteria": {...}}. criteria may contain any of these keys, and only these:
    • "employment_status": the applicant's status must equal it.
    • "max_monthly_income": the applicant's monthly_income must be ≤ it.
    • "has_child_in_school": a boolean. The applicant "has a child in school" if some household member has relation "son" or "daughter" and age 7 to 16 inclusive. This fact must equal the criterion, so True requires such a child and False requires none.
    • "min_household_size": household size (the applicant plus everyone in household) must be ≥ it.

An applicant is eligible for a scheme if they meet every criterion the scheme lists (a scheme with empty criteria is open to everyone). Return a dict mapping every applicant id to the sorted list of scheme ids they are eligible for (an empty list if none).

examples.why: A1 is unemployed, earns 0 and has a 10-year-old son, so both schemes. A2 is employed and has no children, so neither.
B1 plus 2 household members is size 3, so family. The daughter is 17, outside 7-16, so not school. all has no criteria.

constraints: ids are unique strings; 0 ≤ age ≤ 120; 0 ≤ income ≤ 10^6

think.q: What makes an applicant eligible for one scheme?
think.a: Every key in that scheme's criteria must pass. Keys that are missing are not checked. So a scheme is an AND of up to 4 small tests, and an empty criteria dict means "yes".

think.q: Applicant: unemployed, income 0, one son aged 10. Scheme: {"has_child_in_school": True, "max_monthly_income": 2000}?
think.a: Child in school: the son is 10, inside 7-16, so the fact is True, which matches. Income 0 ≤ 2000 passes. Both pass, so eligible.

think.q: What is the first thing you would write?
think.a: Loop schemes, then applicants, re-scan the household for every check, and push passing (applicant, scheme) pairs into one list. Then, to build the answer, scan the whole pair list once per applicant. That last step is O(applicants × pairs), which is quadratic.

"for each applicant", "map id to schemes" → hashing: build the result dict keyed by applicant id as you go, so there is no second search. Also compute each applicant's facts (household size, has a school-age child) once and reuse them for every scheme. A dict from criterion key to a small rule function keeps each rule in one place.

1. facts(a): status, income, 1 + len(household), and any son/daughter aged 7-16.
  2. RULES = {key: lambda f, v: ...}, one per criterion.
  3. For each applicant: compute facts once; keep scheme ids where all(RULES[k](f, v) for k, v in criteria.items()).
  4. result[a["id"]] = sorted(ids).

Ages 6 and 17 (just outside), 7 and 16 (just inside). A spouse or grandchild aged 10 (not a son/daughter). Income exactly equal to the max (eligible). Household size forgetting to count the applicant. "has_child_in_school": False for an applicant who has a school-age child. No schemes (every applicant maps to []). No applicants ({}).

hints: Write a helper that turns one applicant into a few plain facts: status, income, household size (remember to add 1), and whether there is a son or daughter aged 7 to 16.
Map each criterion key to a tiny check, e.g. RULES = {"max_monthly_income": lambda f, v: f["income"] <= v, ...}. Then a scheme passes if all(RULES[k](f, v) for k, v in criteria.items()).
Build the answer dict directly: result[a["id"]] = sorted(passing_ids). Do not collect pairs and search them afterwards.
explain:
Turn each applicant into facts once, then test those facts against each scheme with a lookup table of rules.

  • A1: facts are status unemployed, income 0, size 2, school child True (son, 10).
    • retrenchment: status matches. Eligible.
    • student-aid: school child True == True, 0 ≤ 2000. Eligible.
  • A2: status employed, income 3000, size 1, school child False. Fails status for retrenchment; fails the child rule for student-aid.

The RULES table is what the interviewer is looking for in a take-home: adding a new criterion (say, "has_elderly") is one new fact and one new rule, not a new branch in five places. The facts step is also where you would unit-test the tricky boundaries (age 7 and 16, size counting the applicant). Building result directly as a dict avoids the quadratic "collect pairs, then search" approach.
complexity: O(total household members + applicants * schemes * criteria) time, O(applicants * schemes) for the output

tests.label: example 2
tests.why: household size counts the applicant; age 17 is not in school

tests.label: no schemes
tests.why: every applicant maps to an empty list

tests.label: income at and just above the cap
tests.why: the cap is inclusive: 2,000 passes, 2,001 does not

tests.label: school ages 6, 7, 16, 17
tests.why: only 7 and 16 are inside the inclusive range

tests.label: not a son or daughter
tests.why: a sister, grandson or nephew aged 7-16 does not count, so the applicant has no child in school

tests.label: has_child_in_school False excludes
tests.why: False is a real condition, not "not checked": an applicant with a 9-year-old daughter fails it

tests.label: twins and household size
tests.why: two school-age kids still means true; size is 1 + 3 = 4

tests.label: eight applicants, six schemes
tests.why: every criterion, mixed together, ids sorted

tests.label: zero income, one failing criterion
tests.why: income 0 passes a cap of 0; one failed criterion rejects the scheme

perf.gen: [[{'id': 'P%04d' % i, 'employment_status': 'employed' if i % 3 else 'unemployed', 'household': [{'relation': ['son', 'daughter', 'spouse', 'mother'][j % 4], 'age': (i * 7 + j * 13) % 40} for j in range(i % 6)], 'monthly_income': (i * 7919) % 6000} for i in range(1000)], [{'id': 'S%d' % s, 'criteria': [{'max_monthly_income': 3000}, {'employment_status': 'unemployed', 'max_monthly_income': 4000}, {'has_child_in_school': True}, {'min_household_size': 3}, {'employment_status': 'employed', 'has_child_in_school': True, 'min_household_size': 4, 'max_monthly_income': 5000}][s % 5]} for s in range(10)]]

govtech.source: GovTech take-home: Financial Assistance Scheme eligibility API
govtech.evidence: Public candidate repos describe a GovTech take-home to build a Financial Assistance Scheme management API that returns the schemes an applicant is eligible for; the criteria format and rules here are ours and simplified.
extensions: Expose it as an API: GET /api/schemes/eligible?applicant={id}, plus CRUD for applicants and schemes. Design the tables: applicants, household_members, schemes, and how criteria are stored (JSON column vs one row per rule).
Add a new criterion without editing the loop, e.g. "has_elderly_member": true (anyone aged 65+). With a rules table this is one fact and one entry.
Support OR and nested conditions, e.g. "unemployed OR income ≤ 1,500". How would you represent a rule tree in JSON and evaluate it?
Return why an applicant is not eligible ("income 3,000 is above the 2,000 limit"), so a caseworker can explain the decision.
Schemes change over time. How do you keep past decisions explainable when a scheme's criteria are edited? (Version the criteria and store which version each decision used.)
